title: Ha'azinu: like rain (Deuteronomy 32:2)
hookLine: "My doctrine shall drop as the rain", softly and over time

cards: A cloudburst and a long drizzle can drop the same amount of water. But after a cloudburst, much of it runs off. The ground is hard, the water comes too fast, and it rushes into the gutters.
After a slow, soft rain, the soil drinks most of it in. Any gardener can tell you this. Moses, beginning his last song, says that's exactly how he wants his teaching to arrive.

teach.b: "My doctrine shall drop as the rain, My speech shall distil as the dew; As the small rain upon the tender grass, And as the showers upon the herb." Four pictures of water, each one gentle. Rain.
Dew. Small rain on tender grass. Showers on the herb.
The Hebrew word behind doctrine is likchi, my teaching, from a root that means to take, to receive. Teaching is something received. Notice the pace of the verse.
Rain doesn't fall all at once. Dew arrives overnight, drop by drop, and nobody sees it come. Tender grass can't take a flood.
Moses is describing how teaching lands: slowly, in amounts a listener can hold, over time. The rabbis often compare Torah to water.
The Talmud, in Taanit, says: just as water flows down from a high place to a low one, Torah settles in a person who is humble. And the Sifrei gives another picture.

teach.h: ONE RAIN, EACH PLANT ITS OWN WAY.
teach.b: The same rain falls on the whole field, and each plant grows in its own way: the vine one way, the olive another, the fig another.
The same teaching, falling on different people, helps each one grow into who they are. Patient teachers work this way. They don't pour everything out in one class.
They come back week after week, a little at a time, and wait for it to soak in.

how: Jewish teachers often cite this verse, and the rabbinic comparison of Torah to water, to describe patient, gradual learning, such as the weekly cycle of Torah reading and daily study.

o: be still: Moses calling for silence
remember: the song's call to the past
give ear: the song's opening call to listen

games.q: inside the rain — tap the pairs.
p: Torah settles in the humble, like water
one rain, each plant grows its own way

s: the verse compares teaching to a sudden flood
rain, dew, small rain, showers: gentle and gradual.
the Talmud compares Torah to water that flows to low places
Taanit 7a: it settles in the humble.

games.q: you have a lot to teach a new learner and very little time. what does the verse's picture suggest?
o: pour it all out in one long session.
give it gently, a little at a time.
games.why: rain and dew: teaching that comes softly, in amounts the ground can drink.

practice: Think of someone you're trying to teach, or help, or change, a child, a new coworker, a partner, maybe yourself, and ask whether you've been pouring it on.
Picture a slow rain instead: the smallest piece you could offer, one sentence or one patient answer, with the rest left for another day to soak in.

wordCard.voice: Ha'azinu. Give ear. And the song's second verse: teaching that falls like rain and settles like dew.
